q: What is the product of the Diels–Alder reaction shown?
h: A Diels–Alder makes a six-membered ring with the new C=C between the old C2 and C3 of the diene, and it is stereospecific for the dienophile.
w: The diene's C1 and C4 bond to the two dienophile carbons, forming a cyclohexene whose C=C sits between the old diene C2 and C3, two carbons away from each ring-fusion carbon. Maleic anhydride is a cis dienophile and the reaction is a concerted suprafacial addition, so the two carbonyl groups stay cis: the product is cis-4-cyclohexene-1,2-dicarboxylic anhydride (a meso compound).
x: The trans-fused anhydride would require the dienophile substituents to change their relationship; a concerted [4+2] keeps cis groups cis.
Here the C=C is next to a ring-fusion carbon; in a Diels–Alder adduct the new π bond is between the old diene C2 and C3, flanked by two CH<sub>2</sub> groups.
This cyclobutane is a [2+2] product, which is thermally forbidden; butadiene and maleic anhydride give the six-membered [4+2] ring.

q: 1,3-Butadiene reacts with dimethyl fumarate (dimethyl (E)-but-2-enedioate). What is the product? (For a racemic product only one enantiomer is drawn.)
h: The geometry of the dienophile is kept in the product: groups trans on the alkene end up trans on the ring.
w: The Diels–Alder is stereospecific: both new σ bonds form on the same face of the dienophile at once, so substituents that are trans on the C=C end up trans on the ring. Dimethyl fumarate therefore gives racemic trans-dimethyl cyclohex-4-ene-1,2-dicarboxylate (the (1R,2R) enantiomer is drawn).
x: The cis diester (meso) comes from dimethyl maleate, the Z dienophile, not from fumarate.
A 1,4-cyclohexadiene forms when the dienophile is an alkyne such as dimethyl acetylenedicarboxylate, not an alkene.
The two esters come from two different carbons of the dienophile, so they end up on adjacent ring carbons, not on the same carbon.

q: (2E,4E)-Hexa-2,4-diene reacts with maleic anhydride. What is the relationship of the two methyl groups in the adduct?
c: Cis to each other, whether the adduct is endo or exo
Trans to each other, whether the adduct is endo or exo
Cis in the endo adduct but trans in the exo adduct
A 1:1 mixture of cis and trans, because the diene can rotate during the reaction
h: Classify each methyl as an 'outside' or 'inside' group in the s-cis diene. Do two outside groups end up on the same face or opposite faces?
w: In the s-cis conformation of the (E,E)-diene both methyls point 'outside'. As the diene termini rotate to bond to the dienophile, both outside groups swing toward the same face of the new ring, so they end up cis to each other. Endo vs exo only changes where the anhydride sits relative to the methyls, not the methyl–methyl relationship; the concerted reaction leaves no chance for rotation. (An (E,Z)-diene, with one outside and one inside methyl, would give trans methyls.)
x: Trans methyls come from a diene with one outside and one inside methyl, the (2E,4Z) isomer.
The diene's own stereochemistry fixes the methyl relationship; endo/exo selectivity affects only the dienophile substituents relative to them.
The reaction is concerted, with no intermediate in which a bond could rotate, so it is stereospecific.

q: (E)-1-Methoxy-1,3-butadiene reacts with acrolein (propenal). What is the major constitutional product (ignore stereochemistry)?
h: Find the most nucleophilic diene carbon (use a resonance form that puts negative charge on carbon) and the most electrophilic dienophile carbon. Bond those two.
w: Resonance donation from OCH3 on C1 puts the most negative charge (largest HOMO coefficient) on C4 of the diene. In acrolein, the β carbon (the CH2) is the electrophilic end. Bonding diene C4 to the dienophile CH2 places the CHO-bearing carbon next to the OCH3-bearing carbon: the 'ortho' (1,2) product, 2-methoxycyclohex-3-ene-1-carbaldehyde.
x: This is the 'meta' (1,3) isomer, which forms from the mismatched orientation and is minor.
This 'para' (1,4) pattern with OCH<sub>3</sub> on the ring C=C is what a 2-substituted diene gives; a 1-substituted diene puts the OCH<sub>3</sub> on an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon.
Here the ring C=C is not next to the OCH<sub>3</sub> carbon; in the adduct the diene C1 (bearing OCH<sub>3</sub>) is allylic to the new C=C.

q: 2-Methoxy-1,3-butadiene reacts with methyl acrylate. What is the major constitutional product (ignore stereochemistry)?
h: With a donor on C2 of the diene, which terminal carbon is most electron-rich? Bond it to the β carbon of the acrylate.
w: An OCH3 on C2 pushes electron density to C1 (the CH2 attached to C2). C1 bonds to the electrophilic β carbon (CH2) of methyl acrylate, so the ester-bearing carbon bonds to C4. Counting around the ring, the OCH3 carbon and the CO2CH3 carbon are 1,4 (the 'para' rule for 2-substituted dienes): methyl 4-methoxycyclohex-3-ene-1-carboxylate.
x: This is the 1,3 ('meta') isomer, the minor orientation for a 2-substituted diene.
A 1,2 relationship between the OCH<sub>3</sub> carbon and the ester carbon is impossible here: the diene C2 is on the new C=C, and the dienophile carbons attach only to C1 and C4.
The OCH<sub>3</sub> was on C2 of the diene, which becomes part of the new ring C=C, so it must be on an sp<sup>2</sup> carbon, not an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon.

q: Which diene does not undergo a Diels–Alder reaction with maleic anhydride, even on heating?
h: The diene must reach the s-cis conformation. Look for a diene whose ring holds it permanently in the other conformation.
w: A Diels–Alder needs the diene in the s-cis conformation so C1 and C4 can reach the dienophile together. In 3-methylenecyclohexene the single bond between the two C=C bonds is part of the ring, and the ring locks the exocyclic CH2 and the ring C=C s-trans, so it cannot react.
x: Cyclopentadiene is locked s-cis and is one of the most reactive dienes known.
1,2-Dimethylenecyclohexane holds both exocyclic C=C bonds s-cis, which makes it a reactive diene.
(E)-1,3-Pentadiene rotates freely about C2–C3 and can adopt the s-cis conformation; its methyl is on the outside, so it reacts readily.

q: Rank dienes I–III by their rate of Diels–Alder reaction with maleic anhydride, slowest first.
h: Ask how easily each diene reaches the s-cis conformation, and what is pointing into the space between C1 and C4 when it does.
w: Rate depends on how much s-cis diene is available. III (cyclopentadiene) is held s-cis by its ring, so it is fastest. II, the (E,E) isomer, has both methyls outside and reaches s-cis easily. I, the (Z,Z) isomer, has both methyls 'inside'; in the s-cis form they collide, so very little reactive conformer exists and it is extremely slow. Order: I < II < III.
x: The (Z,Z) diene suffers inside-methyl clash in the s-cis form, so it is slower than the (E,E) diene, not faster.
This is the reverse order; a diene locked s-cis reacts fastest.
An acyclic diene that must rotate into the s-cis form cannot outrun cyclopentadiene, which is permanently s-cis.

q: Cyclopentadiene and maleic anhydride react at room temperature to give mainly the endo adduct. Which description of the endo adduct is correct?
c: The anhydride ring points toward the two-carbon C=C bridge, anti to the one-carbon CH<sub>2</sub> bridge
The anhydride ring points toward the CH<sub>2</sub> bridge, anti to the C=C bridge
The anhydride carbonyls are trans to each other, one on each face of the ring
The anhydride ring is attached at the CH<sub>2</sub> bridge carbon (C7)
h: 'Endo' describes where the dienophile's electron-withdrawing groups sat in the transition state: under the diene π system.
w: In the endo transition state the anhydride carbonyls lie under the diene, where their π orbitals overlap with the developing C2=C3 π bond (secondary orbital interaction). In the norbornene product those diene carbons become the C5=C6 bridge, so the anhydride ring points toward the C=C bridge and away from (anti to) the CH2 bridge. The endo product forms faster even though the exo adduct is slightly more stable.
x: That is the exo adduct, in which the anhydride points toward the CH<sub>2</sub> bridge; it is the minor kinetic product.
Maleic anhydride is a cis dienophile, so both carbonyl carbons stay cis in either the endo or exo adduct.
The dienophile carbons bond to the diene termini (C1 and C4 of the diene), becoming C2 and C3 of the norbornene; C7 is the original CH<sub>2</sub> of cyclopentadiene.

q: Cyclopentadiene reacts with methyl acrylate at 0 °C. Which describes the major product? (Each product forms as a racemate.)
c: the endo adduct: CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> on the face syn to the C=C (anti to the CH<sub>2</sub> bridge)
the exo adduct: CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> on the face syn to the CH<sub>2</sub> bridge (anti to the C=C)
a bicyclo[2.2.2]octene: CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> at C2, with a two-carbon CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub> bridge
a bicyclo[2.2.1]heptene: CO<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> on the one-carbon bridge (C7)
h: First choose the correct ring skeleton (cyclopentadiene gives a bicyclo[2.2.1]heptene with the substituent at C2). Then decide which face the ester ends up on.
w: Cyclopentadiene's CH2 becomes the one-carbon bridge (C7) of a bicyclo[2.2.1]hept-5-ene, and the acrylate carbons become C2 and C3. Under the endo rule (secondary orbital overlap) the ester lies under the diene in the transition state, so in the product it points toward the C5=C6 bridge and away from C7. The major product is the endo adduct, methyl bicyclo[2.2.1]hept-5-ene-2-carboxylate with CO2CH3 syn to the C=C and anti to the CH2 bridge; its diastereomer with the ester syn to the CH2 bridge is the exo adduct.
x: This is the exo diastereomer, with the ester pointing toward the CH<sub>2</sub> bridge. The endo rule makes it the minor kinetic product.
A bicyclo[2.2.2]octene would come from 1,3-cyclohexadiene, which has one more ring carbon than cyclopentadiene.
The ester cannot end up on the one-carbon bridge; C7 comes from the CH<sub>2</sub> of cyclopentadiene, which forms no new bond.

q: Which diene and dienophile would give this compound as the major Diels–Alder product?
h: The cyclohexene C=C came from diene C2–C3; the two sp<sup>3</sup> carbons across the ring came from the dienophile. Then check the regiochemistry against the 'para' rule.
w: Retro-Diels–Alder: break the two σ bonds that are allylic to the ring C=C, on the side opposite the double bond. The four carbons C=C plus its two allylic CH2 neighbors are the diene, with the methyl on an internal (C2) carbon: isoprene. The remaining two carbons, one bearing C≡N, are acrylonitrile. The 1,4 ('para') relationship of CH3 and CN is exactly what a 2-substituted diene gives, so the answer is isoprene + acrylonitrile.
x: 1,3-Pentadiene has its methyl on a terminal carbon, so the methyl would end up on an sp<sup>3</sup> ring carbon, not on the C=C.
Methacrylonitrile would put CH<sub>3</sub> and CN on the same sp<sup>3</sup> carbon, and the ring C=C would have no methyl.
But-2-enenitrile would put CH<sub>3</sub> and CN on adjacent sp<sup>3</sup> carbons, not CH<sub>3</sub> on the alkene.

q: Which diene and dienophile combine to give this bicyclic compound (ignore stereochemistry)?
h: Count the carbons in each bridge. The bridge containing the C=C and the two bridgeheads came from the diene's four π carbons.
w: The compound is a bicyclo[2.2.2]oct-2-ene with CN on a saturated bridge. A cyclic diene gives a bridged product: its four π carbons become the two bridgeheads and the new C=C bridge, and its remaining CH2CH2 becomes a two-carbon bridge, so the diene is 1,3-cyclohexadiene; the CN-bearing two-carbon bridge came from acrylonitrile.
x: Cyclopentadiene has only one extra CH<sub>2</sub>, so it gives a bicyclo[2.2.1]heptene with a one-carbon bridge.
1,4-Cyclohexadiene is not conjugated, so it cannot act as the diene.
An alkyne dienophile would leave a second C=C in the product (a bicyclo[2.2.2]octadiene), but this product has only one.

q: Cyclopentadiene is sold as its dimer, C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>12</sub>. To get the monomer, the dimer is heated to about 170 °C and cyclopentadiene is distilled off. What reaction regenerates the monomer?
h: The dimer formed when one cyclopentadiene acted as a diene and another as a dienophile.
w: At room temperature one cyclopentadiene molecule acts as the diene and a second acts as the dienophile, giving dicyclopentadiene by a Diels–Alder reaction. Heating reverses it: a retro-Diels–Alder breaks the two σ bonds formed in the dimerization. Distilling the volatile monomer (bp 41 °C) pulls the equilibrium toward it.
x: A Cope rearrangement converts one 1,5-diene into another; it does not split a molecule in two.
A 4π electrocyclic opening breaks one σ bond of a cyclobutene; the dimer has no cyclobutene.
A [1,5] H shift moves a hydrogen within one cyclopentadiene; it does not separate two molecules.

q: What is the product when 1,3-butadiene is heated with dimethyl acetylenedicarboxylate (DMAD)?
h: An alkyne dienophile uses only one of its two π bonds. Where does the remaining one end up?
w: The diene forms its usual new C=C between C2 and C3, and the alkyne's second π bond is left in the ring between the two ester-bearing carbons. The product is dimethyl cyclohexa-1,4-diene-1,2-dicarboxylate, with two non-conjugated ring C=C bonds separated by CH2 groups.
x: Dimethyl phthalate would need an extra oxidation (loss of H<sub>2</sub>); the Diels–Alder alone stops at the 1,4-cyclohexadiene.
In this 1,3-diene the two ring C=C bonds are conjugated, but the [4+2] leaves CH<sub>2</sub> groups between them.
This is the adduct of an alkene dienophile (dimethyl maleate); an alkyne leaves a C=C between the ester carbons.

q: In a normal-electron-demand Diels–Alder reaction (electron-rich diene, electron-poor dienophile), which frontier-orbital interaction dominates?
c: HOMO of the diene (ψ<sub>2</sub>) with LUMO of the dienophile (π*)
HOMO of the dienophile (π) with HOMO of the diene (ψ<sub>2</sub>)
LUMO of the diene (ψ<sub>3</sub>) with LUMO of the dienophile (π*)
ψ<sub>1</sub> of the diene with LUMO of the dienophile (π*)
h: A stabilizing two-electron interaction pairs a filled orbital with an empty one. Electron-donating groups raise orbitals; electron-withdrawing groups lower them.
w: Bonding interactions come from a filled orbital mixing with an empty one, and the smaller the energy gap, the stronger the interaction. Donor groups raise the diene HOMO (ψ2) and withdrawing groups lower the dienophile LUMO (π*), making that gap small. So diene HOMO (ψ2) + dienophile LUMO (π*) controls the rate and regiochemistry; the terminal lobes of ψ2 and π* match in phase on the same face, so the reaction is thermally allowed.
x: Two filled orbitals mixing (HOMO + HOMO) gives no net bonding; it is a four-electron, repulsive interaction.
Two empty orbitals mixing contributes no electrons, so it cannot form bonds.
ψ<sub>1</sub> is filled but much lower in energy than ψ<sub>2</sub>, so its gap to π* is large and its interaction is weak.

q: Furan and maleic anhydride give mainly the endo adduct after a few minutes at room temperature, but after a long reaction time the isolated product is almost entirely the exo adduct. Which explanation fits?
c: The adducts revert readily to furan + maleic anhydride, so the more stable exo adduct accumulates under equilibrium
The endo adduct isomerizes to exo by rotation about the new C–C σ bonds
Secondary orbital overlap favors the exo transition state once the furan becomes aromatic
Furan reacts only through its s-trans conformation, which gives the exo product
h: Furan loses its aromatic stabilization when it reacts. How does that affect the reverse reaction?
w: Furan is aromatic, so its Diels–Alder adducts are only modestly downhill and the retro-Diels–Alder is fast even at room temperature. The endo adduct forms faster (kinetic control, secondary orbital overlap), but it keeps reverting. Over time the system reaches equilibrium and the more stable exo adduct accumulates (thermodynamic control).
x: Converting endo to exo would require breaking a ring bond; bond rotation within the bicyclic framework cannot do it.
Secondary orbital overlap favors the endo transition state; it never favors exo.
Furan's ring locks its diene s-cis; an s-trans diene cannot do a Diels–Alder at all.

q: Rank dienophiles I–III by Diels–Alder reactivity toward cyclopentadiene, slowest first.
h: Electron-withdrawing groups lower the dienophile LUMO, bringing it closer to the diene HOMO.
w: In a normal-demand Diels–Alder the dienophile is the electrophile, and each electron-withdrawing group lowers its LUMO. Ethylene has none and reacts only under forcing conditions; methyl acrylate has one ester; tetracyanoethylene has four cyano groups and reacts almost instantly. Order: I < II < III.
x: This is the reverse order; electron-withdrawing groups speed up the reaction rather than slow it.
Ethylene has no activating group, so it is slower than methyl acrylate.
Four cyano groups make tetracyanoethylene far more electron-poor than methyl acrylate, so it is faster.

q: In the Diels–Alder reaction of 1,3-butadiene with ethylene, how many π bonds are broken and how many new σ bonds are formed?
c: 3 π bonds broken; 2 new C–C σ bonds and 1 new π bond formed
2 π bonds broken; 2 new C–C σ bonds formed
3 π bonds broken; 3 new C–C σ bonds formed
2 π bonds broken; 1 new C–C σ bond and 1 new π bond formed
h: Count all π bonds in the reactants and all π bonds in cyclohexene.
w: The reactants have three π bonds (two in butadiene, one in ethylene). The product cyclohexene has one new π bond (between the old diene C2 and C3) and two new C–C σ bonds that close the ring. So three π bonds are broken, and two σ bonds plus one new π bond are formed. Trading two π bonds for two stronger σ bonds is why the reaction is exothermic.
x: Butadiene's two π bonds and ethylene's one π bond are all broken, which is three, not two.
Only two σ bonds are needed to close the six-membered ring; the third electron pair becomes the new π bond.
Two σ bonds form, not one; the ring has two new connections, C1–C6 and C4–C5.
